Volatility Factor Project: overview¶

This notebook walks through the volatility_factor package end to end, from configuration and pricing data through model estimation, simulation, the production run, backtesting and quarterly monitoring. Every example runs against the project's real configuration and pricing data.

It describes functionality, not operating procedure. See GARCH Simulation - Volatility Factor - MDA Departmental Procedures for production steps and GARCH Simulation - Technical Documentation for the model.

Contents

  1. Overview
  2. Setup: finding the config and pricing data
  3. Configuration
  4. Pricing data and price-observation QA
  5. VarData: prices, returns and portfolios
  6. GarchSim: estimation
  7. GarchSim: simulation and VaR
  8. NonParametricVar: circular block bootstrap
  9. The production run
  10. Backtesting
  11. Quarterly monitoring
  12. Testing and validation

1. Overview¶

The project is a Python package (volatility_factor), a configuration file (configs/var_config_volfactor.yml) and pricing data (data/pricing_data_combined.csv). Users change the configuration file and run notebooks/volatility_factor_main.ipynb to produce the volatility factors; the other notebooks backtest and monitor them.

A production run flows like this:

config (factors, windows, settings) ─┐
                                     ├─► GarchSim per factor & window ─► VaR results ─► saved .xlsx / .parquet
pricing data (+ QA report) ──────────┘                                       │
                                                                             ├─► run_backtests ─► exceptions, independence tests
                                                                             └─► monitoring ────► F-tests, exception counts, shortfalls

Package modules

Module What it holds
config Config (the YAML file), FactorConfig, GarchSettings; get_config / set_config / use_config
data PricingData (prices from CSV, parquet or a DataFrame) and its QA report; VarData (prices and returns for an index or portfolio)
garch GarchSim (GARCH(1,1) fitting and simulation) and GarchFit (one fitted model with the full arch result)
nonparametric NonParametricVar (circular block bootstrap)
periods sample / forecast windows and stress-window selection
pipeline run_garch_var and run_circular_bootstrap: every configured factor in one call
backtesting VarBacktest, log_likelihood_test (Kupiec / Christoffersen) and run_backtests
monitoring quarterly F-tests, exception counts and shortfalls
plotting Plotly charts (every chart returns a figure)
results VaRResult (a simulation's results) and to_long

The API is built for method chaining: settings methods return the object, and charts return Plotly figures, e.g. VarData.from_id("agy_cmo").garch(start, end).simulate(...).

In [1]:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import plotly.io as pio

import volatility_factor as vf
from volatility_factor import (
    GarchSim,
    MonitoringPeriods,

    PricingData,

    monitoring,
)

pio.renderers.default = "plotly_mimetype+notebook_connected"
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 30)

pd.set_option("display.precision", 4)

# Example outputs in this notebook are written here, never to the project's output folder.
OUT = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="volfactor_overview_"))

2. Setup: finding the config and pricing data¶

Install the package once (from the repository root):

pip install -e ".[dev]"

Nothing is read when the package is imported. The config and pricing data are found the first time they are needed:

What Lookup order
Config config= argument → vf.set_config() / vf.use_config() → $VOLFACTOR_CONFIG → configs/var_config_volfactor.yml in the working directory or any parent
Pricing data data= argument → vf.set_data() / vf.use_data() → $VOLFACTOR_DATA → data_settings.pricing_data in the config

Relative paths in the config file are relative to the config file itself, so notebooks work from any folder. A price file loaded by path is read once and shared by every model.

In [2]:
cfg = vf.get_config()
data = vf.get_data()
print("Config:      ", cfg.path)
print("Pricing data:", data)
print("Outputs go to", cfg.output_file)

Outputs go to C:\Users\aarba\pydev\VolatilityFactor\.claude\worktrees\volatility-factor-refactor-6ac40b\output\combined_vars_2024-12-31.xlsx

To test with a different price file (same format, different data), pass it to a single model, or swap it in for a block of code:

In [3]:
sample = PricingData.from_csv("../tests/fixtures/pricing_sample.csv")  # a small extract

print(VarData("CMOS", data=sample).data)    # one model
with vf.use_data(sample):                   # everything inside the block
    print(VarData("CMOS").data)
print(VarData("CMOS").data)                 # back to the default

3. Configuration¶

configs/var_config_volfactor.yml has three sections:

  • data_settings: the pricing data file, the output folder and the output file name.
  • garch_settings: simulation sizes, sample and forecast windows, the VaR types to run (long_term, normal, short_term, stress_var) and the starting-value quantiles.
  • var_settings: one entry per volatility factor: its tickers, weights and liquidation periods (ndays). The entry's key is the factor's volatility_factor_id.
In [4]:
cfg.garch
Out[4]:
GarchSettings(last_sample_date='2024-12-31', horizon1=63, horizon2=252, nsims=10000, number_of_periods=3, sample_years=9, forecast_months=12, forecast_lag=3, var_type=('long_term',), start_point_quantiles=(0.5,))

periods() turns garch_settings into sample windows and their forecast windows (most recent first). Each sample is sample_years long; its forecast starts forecast_lag months after the sample ends and runs for forecast_months.

Price-observation QA¶

coverage_report() summarises each index's price history to find incomplete pricing before it reaches a model.

  • Expected dates are the vendor's (Source) pricing dates between the index's first and last price. A vendor pricing date is one on which at least half of that vendor's live indices are priced, so vendor holidays and sporadic dates (such as weekend month-end marks) are not counted as missing.
  • Flags (Status = "Review"): missing vendor dates, gaps longer than max_gap_days while the vendor priced other indices, runs of stale_days or more unchanged prices, duplicate or invalid dates, missing sources, missing or invalid prices, and prices that stop early.
  • Informational: LargestGapDays, WeekendObservations and StartsLate (usually the index's inception).

5. VarData: prices, returns and portfolios¶

VarData is the base of every model. It holds one index or a weighted portfolio and computes prices, returns and descriptions as cached properties (calculated on first access).

  • tickers accepts a string, list or tuple.
  • weights must sum to one. None means equal weights. A single index always has weight 1.
  • VarData.from_id(...) takes the tickers and weights from the config.
In [15]:
print(VarData("CMOS").weights)                                     # single index
print(VarData(["G6P0", "G9P0"]).weights)                           # equal weights
print(VarData(["G1P0", "G2P0", "CMOS"], [0.5, 0.3, 0.2]).weights)  # given weights
print(VarData("CMOS", weights=2).weights)                          # ignored for one index
try:
    VarData(["G6P0", "G9P0"], [0.6, 0.6])
except ValueError as exc:
    print("ValueError:", exc)

6. GarchSim: estimation¶

GarchSim fits one GARCH(1,1) model with normal errors (and, by default, a zero mean) to each constituent's daily log returns over the sample window, using the ARCH package.

  • Scaling. Returns are multiplied by a scale before fitting to help the optimiser. 1,000 is tried first, then 10,000, 100 and 10 until the fit converges.
  • Lazy fitting. Models are fitted the first time a fitted value is used, or when fit() is called. Changing the sample window clears the fit.
  • Full arch results. Each fit is a GarchFit in fits[ticker]. It exposes every attribute of the arch result directly (fit.params, fit.aic, fit.summary(), fit.forecast(...) …), plus the scale used and every attempt.
In [22]:
gsim = GarchSim.from_id("agy_cmo", sample_start="2016-01-01", sample_end="2024-12-31").fit()
gsim.summary()

7. GarchSim: simulation and VaR¶

Once the models are fitted, simulate() generates forward-looking one-day price paths from them. The one-day paths are turned into n-day changes as set out in the model documentation. The first horizon1 days are a lag and are dropped; VaR is measured over the next horizon2 days (usually 252 + ndays - 1).

The simulation type is chosen with shock_type:

1. normal: shocks are drawn from a standard normal distribution for the whole forecast (horizon1 + horizon2 days).

2. custom_normal: the process used for the long-term VaR, the volatility factor used for the annual review period. It is identical to normal, except that the shocks for periods 64 to 68 (the first five days after the lag) are multiplied by $\sqrt{2}$. See section 3.3.1 of the GARCH Simulation - Technical Documentation.

3. bootstrap: instead of normal draws, shocks are resampled from the fitted standardized residuals in a user-defined window (bootstrap_start, bootstrap_end).

4. custom_bootstrap: combines the two: shocks for the first horizon1 periods are resampled from the fitted residuals in the bootstrap window; the rest are standard normal draws.

For a portfolio, normal shocks are drawn with the constituents' correlation, and bootstrap shocks resample whole days so constituents move together.

Starting values¶

By default (start_vals=None) the simulation starts from the last fitted residual and volatility in the sample. To choose them, pass start_vals=(date, quantile): a one-day variance forecast is made for each business day from date to the sample end, and the starting values are taken from the day at that quantile of the forecasts (for a portfolio, the quantile of portfolio volatility). For the long-term VaR, the starting values are the 50th percentile of the one-day variance forecast over the last year of the sample.

In [28]:
h1, ndays, nsims = 63, 10, 10_000
h2 = 252 + ndays - 1
start_vals = ("2024-01-01", 0.50)
boot = {"bootstrap_start": "2024-07-01", "bootstrap_end": "2024-12-31"}

rows = []
for shock in ["normal", "custom_normal", "bootstrap", "custom_bootstrap"]:
    for sv in [None, start_vals]:
        extra = boot if "bootstrap" in shock else {}
        rows.append(gsim.simulate(h1, h2, ndays, shock, nsims, start_vals=sv, **extra).to_dict())

pd.DataFrame(rows)[["Method", "ShockType", "StartingValueQ", "BootstrapStart", "BootstrapEnd",
                    "VaR_50", "VaR_75", "VaR_95", "VaR_99"]]

simulate() returns a VaRResult. It works like a dict of the result columns and also keeps the simulated paths:

  • record / to_dict() / to_frame(): the result columns.
  • var(level), log_var(level): arithmetic and log VaR at 0.50, 0.75, 0.95 or 0.99.
  • sim_paths: simulated one-day portfolio log returns (nsims × (horizon1 + horizon2)).
  • nday_returns: rolling n-day sums of the forecast part of each path.
  • var_by_path: each path's VaR; the reported VaR values are percentiles of these across paths.
In [29]:
res = gsim.simulate(h1, h2, ndays, "custom_normal", nsims, start_vals=start_vals)
print(res)
print("VaR 99:", res["VaR_99"], "| VaR 95:", res.var(0.95), "| log VaR 99:", res.log_var(0.99))
print("paths:", res.sim_paths.shape, "| n-day windows × paths:", res.nday_returns.shape)
res.to_frame()

The starting values and the windows used by the production VaR types can be inspected directly: the short-term VaR bootstraps from the last six months of the sample, and the stress VaR from the most volatile 126-day window (99th percentile).

print("Starting residual / volatility:", gsim.get_single_index_startvals(start_vals))
print("Stress window:", vf.get_stress_range(gsim.training_data, "2016-01-01", "2024-12-31",

8. NonParametricVar: circular block bootstrap¶

A non-parametric check on the GARCH VaR. The sample's weighted log returns are split into overlapping blocks of length √n (wrapping around the end of the sample). Each bootstrap sample strings randomly chosen blocks together; its n-day VaR is computed, and the result is the mean across samples.

In [32]:
npv = NonParametricVar.from_id("agy_cmo", sample_start="2016-01-01", sample_end="2024-12-31")
npv.circular_block_bootstrap(n_liquidation=10, nboot=1_000, var_p=0.99)

9. The production run¶

run_garch_var() runs every factor, liquidation period, sample window and starting-value quantile in the config. For each combination it runs the configured VaR types:

var_type Shock type Bootstrap window Method label
long_term custom_normal – long_term_var_<q>
normal normal – normal_var_<q>
short_term custom_bootstrap last 6 months of the sample short_term_var_<q>
stress_var custom_bootstrap most volatile 126-day window stress_var_<q>

Before simulating, a QA check confirms that prices cover the sample window (within four days at each end). Windows that fail are recorded in qa. If every window is skipped, save() writes the QA workbook and raises an error before publishing VaR results.

In production this is simply vf.run_garch_var().save() (see volatility_factor_main.ipynb). Here it runs for two factors and saves to the temporary folder.

In [33]:
run_cfg = cfg.with_factors("agy_cmo", "G6P0[50];G9P0[50]")
run = vf.run_garch_var(run_cfg, verbose=False)
run.results[["Volatility_Factor_ID", "NDays", "SampleStart", "SampleEnd", "ForecastStart",
             "ForecastEnd", "Method", "ConvergencyCode", "VaR_50", "VaR_99"]]

10. Backtesting¶

VarBacktest compares a VaR level with realised n-day price changes over a window.

  • var is in percent (2.0 means 2%). var_is_log=True treats it as a log return and converts it to an arithmetic one.
  • forward_shift=False dates each n-day change at its end; True dates it at its start.
  • A break (exception) is an n-day change below -var; the shortfall is the change plus the VaR (negative means a break).
In [37]:
bt = VarData("CMOS").backtest(n_liquidation=10, var=2.0, start_date="2022-01-01",
                              end_date="2024-12-31", var_is_log=False)
print("VaR:", f"{bt.var_pct:.2%}", "| observations:", len(bt.nday_price_return),
      "| breaks:", bt.exceptions)
pd.concat({"NDayReturn": bt.nday_price_return, "Break": bt.break_series,
           "Shortfall": bt.shortfall_series}, axis=1).tail()

VaR: 2.00% | observations: 752 | breaks: 76

independence_test() reports the Kupiec unconditional coverage statistic (LR_uc) and the Christoffersen independence and conditional coverage statistics (LR_ind and LR_cc). The report includes the count of usable observations and exceptions. The transition tests condition on the first observation. A window with no usable returns has blank statistics and a blank independence decision. The decision is "RejectNull" when LR_ind exceeds the chi-squared critical value.

In [38]:
bt.independence_test(converge_rate=0.01, alpha=0.99)
Out[38]:

Settings can be changed in place; cached results are recalculated:

In [40]:
print("Breaks at 2%:", bt.exceptions)
print("Breaks at 3%:", bt.with_var(3.0).exceptions)
print("Breaks in 2024 at 3%:", bt.with_window("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31").exceptions)

Breaks at 2%: 76
Breaks at 3%: 9
Breaks in 2024 at 3%: 0
In [41]:
bt.with_window("2022-01-01", "2024-12-31").price_change_plot()

run_backtests() and run.backtest() test each VaR quantile over its forecast window. A 95% VaR uses a 5% expected exception rate. The detail is padded through the forecast end by default when pricing stops early. save() writes a parquet file of observations and an Excel workbook of test statistics.

bt_run = run.backtest().save(OUT / run_cfg.output_file.name)

11. Quarterly monitoring¶

MonitoringPeriods describes the windows: the full sample, its last year (used for starting values) and the quarters after the sample.

In [44]:
periods = MonitoringPeriods.from_config(cfg)
periods
Out[44]:
MonitoringPeriods(full=('2016-01-01', '2024-12-31'), start=('2024-01-01', '2024-12-31'), quarters=(('2025-01-01', '2025-03-31'), ('2025-04-01', '2025-06-30'), ('2025-07-01', '2025-09-30'), ('2025-10-01', '2025-12-31'), ('2026-01-01', '2026-03-31')))

F-tests. For each quarter, the variance of out-of-sample returns is compared with the full sample (Q-vs-Full), the last year of the sample (Q-vs-1Y) and the sample's largest rolling variance over the same number of days (Q-vs-Max), each with its critical value (_CV). Columns are prefixed with the quarter number.

In [45]:
mon_cfg = cfg.with_factors("agy_cmo", "G6P0[50];G9P0[50]")
monitoring.f_test_report(periods, quarters=[1, 2, 3], config=mon_cfg)

Exceptions. One-day exceptions are counted per quarter against the one-day 95% VaR. N-day exceptions are counted from the start of quarter 2 through the end of the chosen quarter, with the independence test; when breaks cluster, EXCEPTION_ADJUSTMENT gives the number of exceptions to remove. Portfolios use their configured weights (use_config_weights=False uses equal weights). These examples use 2,000 simulations to run quickly; the monitoring notebook uses 10,000.

In [46]:
monitoring.one_day_exceptions(periods, quarters=[1, 2, 3, 4], nsims=2_000, config=mon_cfg)

12. Testing and validation¶

The package's tests run with:

pytest -m "not regression"   # fast unit tests
pytest -m regression         # checks against reference outputs
  • Regression tests compare fitted models, simulation paths, VaR outputs, backtest details and monitoring reports with checked-in reference fixtures. Reported VaR matches exactly, with tight tolerances for unrounded calculations.
  • Unit tests cover configuration and data lookup, validation, chaining, the price QA report and every chart.

To try a model against different data, run it with another price file, e.g. the test extract:

In [49]:
with vf.use_data(sample):
    check = vf.run_garch_var(cfg.with_factors("agy_cmo").with_garch(nsims=1_000), verbose=False)
check.results[["Volatility_Factor_ID", "NDays", "SampleEnd", "Method", "VaR_99"]]
